reviewSession.heading: Investigations: objective 7.1
reviewSession.body: Let us go back over Domain 7 together, one objective at a time, starting with investigations. The order of volatility is the most tested idea here. Registers and cache come first. Then the routing table, the address cache, running processes and memory. Then temporary files, disk, remote logs, physical layout, and finally archive tapes. People often pick the disk image first, because it feels thorough, but memory disappears when power goes. Next, chain of custody records who held the evidence, when, where and why, with no gaps. Remember that it proves control, not truth. Criminal cases need proof beyond a reasonable doubt, and civil cases need only a preponderance of the evidence. When you choose an answer, protect the original, work on a verified copy, and call in legal early if a court is possible. Do not let a curious manager browse a suspect's computer.

reviewSession.heading: Logging and monitoring: objective 7.2
reviewSession.body: Now for logging and monitoring. Keep this simple picture in mind. An intrusion detection system alerts. An intrusion prevention system sits in the path and blocks. A security information and event management system collects logs, links them and alerts people. A security orchestration tool follows playbooks and acts. Signature detection misses new attacks, and anomaly detection catches them but makes more false alarms. The false negative is the dangerous result, because nobody knows anything happened. When a question describes staff drowning in alarms, the best answer is to tune the rules, never to switch the tool off. Logs must be sent to a central place, protected from change, and given synchronised clocks. Egress monitoring looks at what is leaving, and threat hunting assumes that someone is already inside. User and entity behaviour analytics spots an account doing something unusual, even when every action was technically allowed.

reviewSession.heading: Configuration and change: objectives 7.3 and 7.9
reviewSession.body: Let us take configuration and change management together, because people mix them up. Change management decides whether a change may happen. Configuration management records how things stand and checks that systems match. The baseline is the approved setup, and drift is moving away from it. If a weakness keeps appearing on new machines, fix the golden image and not each machine. The change steps are request, review, approve or reject, test, schedule and implement, and document. Every change needs a rollback plan. A change that worked but was never recorded still failed the process. In an emergency, a named person authorises the change, you act, and then you document and review it afterwards. The correct answer is rarely to do nothing, and rarely to skip the record. If a change has caused an outage, roll back first and ask questions later.

reviewSession.heading: Foundational concepts: objective 7.4
reviewSession.body: Now the foundations. Need to know is about information, and least privilege is about rights. Someone can have the right clearance and still have no need to know. Separation of duties means no one person completes a risky task alone, so fraud now needs collusion. It does not remove collusion. Job rotation and mandatory vacations reveal fraud that needs daily hiding, and rotation also gives cross-training. Privilege creep is what happens when old rights are kept, and access reviews are the cure. Shared administrator accounts destroy accountability, so the fix is individual accounts with recorded sessions. Be ready for a service level agreement calculation. At 99.9 percent of a 720 hour month, about 43 minutes of downtime is allowed. And remember the manager's view. You can hand over the work to a provider, but you never hand over accountability.

reviewSession.heading: Resource protection: objective 7.5
reviewSession.body: Let us move to resource protection. Deleting and formatting do not remove data. Learn clear, purge and destroy, from weakest to strongest. Clear defeats ordinary software tools. Purge defeats a laboratory, and it includes degaussing and cryptographic erase. Destroy means shredding, crushing or burning. The trap that catches people is that degaussing does not work on solid-state drives, so read the type of media carefully. If the data is very sensitive and the drive will not be reused, physical destruction is safest. Check for a legal hold before anything is destroyed, because a court case overrides the retention schedule. Encrypt anything that travels, send the key by another route, and treat a backup with the same care as the live data. Finally, match the control to the state of the data. Full-disk encryption protects data at rest on a powered-off device. It does nothing for data crossing a network.

reviewSession.heading: Incident management: objective 7.6
reviewSession.body: Incident management is one of the most heavily tested areas, so say the seven steps aloud with me. Detection. Response. Mitigation. Reporting. Recovery. Remediation. Lessons learned. When a question asks what comes next, work out which step has just been completed, and choose the very next one. People most often confuse recovery with remediation. Recovery brings the service back. Remediation removes the root cause, so the attacker cannot return the same way. Contain before you repair. Isolate a machine from the network, but leave it running, because memory holds evidence. Never hack back, since that may be illegal and may strike an innocent victim. Reporting has its own place in the list, but in practice it continues all the way through, and legal staff will know the time limits. Hold the lessons learned meeting last, and keep it free of blame.

reviewSession.heading: Detective and preventive measures: objective 7.7
reviewSession.body: Now let us revisit detective and preventive measures. A firewall list should end with implicit deny. A web application firewall reads web requests, and a next-generation firewall understands applications and users. Choose the tool that matches the attack in the question. An allow list blocks anything unknown, so it is stronger, and it suits stable systems. A deny list permits anything unknown, so it suits changing environments. A sandbox lets you watch what a file does, but a clean result is no guarantee. A honeypot must be isolated from real systems. Remember the legal line. Enticement leaves something available, and it is allowed. Entrapment persuades someone to commit a crime, and it is not allowed. Outside providers bring skills and hours, but accountability stays with you. Automated and learning tools help with scale, but people must still review what they produce.

reviewSession.heading: Patch and vulnerability management: objective 7.8
reviewSession.body: Next, patching and vulnerabilities. It all begins with an accurate inventory, because you cannot protect what you do not know about. A scan looks and reports, while a penetration test really tries to get in, and it needs written permission first. The name of a weakness comes from CVE, and its score comes from CVSS. Learn the bands. Low runs from 0.1 to 3.9, medium from 4.0 to 6.9, high from 7.0 to 8.9, and critical from 9.0 to 10.0. The trap is choosing the highest score. Look for facts about exposure, active attacks and business value, because risk decides the order. Test patches before production, send them through change management, and scan again to verify. If no patch exists, use compensating controls. If a system can never be patched, isolate it, and have management accept the remaining risk in writing.

reviewSession.heading: Recovery strategies: objective 7.10
reviewSession.body: Let us go back to recovery strategies, where exact details matter. Incremental backups copy what changed since the last backup of any kind, so a restore needs the full and every incremental in order. Differential backups copy what changed since the last full, so a restore needs the full and only the latest differential. Cold sites have space and power and take weeks. Warm sites have some equipment and older data and take days. Hot sites are fully equipped and take minutes or hours. Now the RAID levels. RAID 0 has two disks minimum and no fault tolerance. RAID 1 has two disks and survives one failure. RAID 5 has three disks and survives one failure. RAID 6 has four disks and survives two. RAID 10 has four disks and survives one failure in each mirrored pair. And RAID is never a backup.

reviewSession.heading: Disaster recovery and testing: objectives 7.11 and 7.12
reviewSession.body: Disaster recovery and its testing belong together. In a real event, people's safety comes first, and then a named person declares the disaster against clear triggers. Keep copies of the plan away from the main site and on paper. Plan several ways of communicating, and use one trained spokesperson. Now the direction of restoration, which people often reverse. Going to the recovery site, bring up the most critical work first. Coming home, move the least critical work first, to prove that the repaired site is stable. Test types run from least to most disruptive: read-through, tabletop, walkthrough, simulation, parallel and full interruption. A new plan starts with a read-through. If the question says the main site must keep running, a full interruption is ruled out. A parallel test gives real proof with no outage risk, and a full interruption needs senior management approval.

reviewSession.heading: Business continuity: objective 7.13
reviewSession.body: Now business continuity. It keeps the whole business working, while disaster recovery restores the technology. Your role on this objective is to participate and advise. The business owners and senior management decide what matters and accept the plan. Senior management support comes first, because without it there is no budget and no authority. The most tested rule is this. The recovery time objective plus the work recovery time must be no more than the maximum tolerable downtime. The recovery point objective is different. It looks backward, and it says how much data you can afford to lose. The trap is an answer that quietly changes a downtime figure so that a cheap option looks acceptable. The right answer is to explain the gap and let the business decide. In an exercise, follow the plan as written, and record every problem instead of quietly working around it.

reviewSession.heading: Physical security and personnel safety: objectives 7.14 and 7.15
reviewSession.body: Finally, physical security and the safety of people. Whenever a choice appears between protecting people and protecting things, people win. Exit doors fail safe, so that nobody is trapped. Fail-secure belongs on rooms where no one can be caught inside. Know the fence heights: three to four feet deters casual walkers, six to seven feet is hard to climb, and eight feet with three strands of barbed wire deters a determined intruder. Bollards stop vehicles, and an access control vestibule stops tailgating. Under duress, comply and raise the alarm silently. When travelling, take a clean device with only the data needed, and treat it with suspicion on return. Awareness training should cover insider threats, social media and repeated login prompts. Never approve a prompt that you did not start. That brings us to the end of this domain. Think like an adviser, put people first, and fix the cause.
